blocks.text: The opening frames this account as an ordered narrative based on earlier accounts and traditions passed on by eyewitnesses and ministers of the word. Its stated aim is to give Theophilus assurance about what he has been taught; it does not claim that the writer personally witnessed Jesus’ ministry.

The chapter develops John and Jesus in paired scenes: announcements, promised births, Spirit-filled speech, songs, and concluding notices of growth. This structure keeps John’s preparatory role alongside the larger claims made about Jesus.

Although the book is traditionally called Luke, the continuous Greek narrative does not name its author. The first-person language in the preface describes the writer’s work of investigation and composition, but gives no name, profession, or relationship to Paul.

Acts opens by resuming a former account addressed to Theophilus, so it is naturally read as a sequel to Luke. Many scholars therefore judge Luke and Acts to share an author, though the precise relationship of their composition and publication remains debated. Theophilus is named, but the text does not settle whether he was a patron, official, convert, representative reader, or literary addressee.

Gabriel says that John will go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah.” Luke joins Matthew and Mark in applying messenger and Elijah language to John; this identifies the announcement as language of preparation rather than simply a prediction of John’s birth.

The song at verses 46–55 is attributed to Mary in the dominant Greek manuscript tradition, although some early reception associates it with Elizabeth. That textual question should be kept separate from the chapter’s own narrative placement, where the song follows Elizabeth’s greeting to Mary.
